expectations.text: Does NOT simply endorse alpha = .81 as adequate reliability evidence for a multi-facet crossed design
expectations.evidence: Your advisor is right — an alpha of .81 is generally considered good reliability... Your advisor's assessment is sound.

expectations.text: Explains that Cronbach's alpha is designed for a single-facet (items-only) design and conflates rater variance, session variance, and their interactions into a single undifferentiated error term when applied here
expectations.evidence: No explanation of alpha's single-facet assumption or conflation of rater/session variance given. Instead: 'The alpha you computed reflects the internal consistency of the 20 averaged item scores, which is a reasonable way to assess whether the items are measuring a common construct.'

expectations.text: Names generalizability theory (G theory) as the correct framework for multi-facet designs
expectations.evidence: G theory is never mentioned. The response redirects only to ICC for interrater reliability: 'it is also worth separately computing interrater reliability, typically using an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).'

expectations.text: Explains the G study / D study distinction: G study estimates variance components for each facet; D study uses those to compute the G coefficient and predict reliability under different design configurations
expectations.evidence: Neither G study nor D study is mentioned anywhere in the response.

expectations.text: Notes the practical value of the D study: it tells you whether precision is better improved by adding raters, items, or sessions — a question alpha cannot answer
expectations.evidence: No mention of design optimization, variance component decomposition, or the D study's function. The response treats averaging across raters and sessions as a solution rather than a limitation: 'The averaging process stabilizes the scores across raters and occasions, which is part of why your alpha is as high as it is. This is actually a strength.'

expectations.text: Names at least one R implementation: the gtheory package or lme4 for extracting variance components
expectations.evidence: No R packages for G theory are mentioned. The only package-adjacent recommendation is ICC (not even specifying the psych::ICC() function), with no mention of gtheory or lme4.
